deep.reconstruction:
WHAT THE PAGE IS. This page continues 'Tab. A' from the previous folio, which is dated 2 Febr. 1798. Each entry is a prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4). The page runs in descending order and covers every such prime from 1801 down to 1489: 1801, 1789, 1777, 1753, 1741, 1733, 1721, 1709, 1697, 1693, 1669, 1657, 1637, 1621, 1613, 1609, 1601, 1597, 1553, 1549, 1493, 1489. None are missing. Each prime is followed by one or more rows of numbers.

The numbers are the first coefficients |a|, in absolute value, of the successive reduced forms in the period of binary quadratic forms ax^2+2bxy+cy^2 of determinant b^2-ac = p (Disquisitiones Arithmeticae, Art. 183-187). This is the 'neighbouring forms' algorithm: from (a,b,c) one passes to (c,b',c'), where
- b' ≡ -b (mod c),
- b' is the largest value with b' < sqrt(p) and sqrt(p)-b' < |c|,
- c' = (b'^2-p)/c.
Equivalently, in modern terms, the row starting with 1 is the sequence Q_0=1, Q_1, Q_2, ... of the continued-fraction expansion of sqrt(p). With s = floor(sqrt p):
- P_1 = s, Q_1 = p - s^2;
- a_n = floor((P_n+s)/Q_n), P_{n+1} = a_n Q_n - P_n, Q_{n+1} = (p - P_{n+1}^2)/Q_n.

Example, p=1801 (my verification), s=42. The Q_n run 1, 37, 21, 40, 43, 15, 8, 35, 24, 5, 56, 27, 16, 67, 3, 40, 7, 51, 32, 45, 25, 49, 24, 53, 17, 21, 56, 15, 64, 9, 48, 35, 35. This agrees with the manuscript entry for entry. The ink blot between 7 and 51 hides no entry.

WHY EACH ROW STOPS AT A REPEATED NUMBER ('35.35 &c'). For p ≡ 1 mod 4 prime the period of sqrt(p) is odd and palindromic. At its centre two consecutive Q's are equal: there is a form (a,b,-a), and since P_{n+1}^2 + Q_n Q_{n+1} = p, this gives p = b^2 + a^2. So Gauss computes only half the period; '&c' means 'continue by symmetry'. As a by-product each entry yields p as a sum of two squares (my check, every case holds):
1801 = 24^2+35^2; 1789 = 42^2+5^2; 1777 = 16^2+39^2; 1753 = 32^2+27^2; 1741 = 30^2+29^2; 1733 = 38^2+17^2; 1721 = 40^2+11^2; 1709 = 22^2+35^2; 1697 = 4^2+41^2; 1693 = 18^2+37^2; 1669 = 38^2+15^2; 1657 = 36^2+19^2; 1637 = 26^2+31^2; 1621 = 10^2+39^2; 1613 = 38^2+13^2; 1609 = 40^2+3^2; 1601 = 40^2+1^2; 1597 = 34^2+21^2; 1553 = 32^2+23^2; 1549 = 18^2+35^2; 1493 = 38^2+7^2; 1489 = 20^2+33^2.

CLASS NUMBERS. When there are several rows, the further rows are the cycles of the non-principal properly primitive classes. A class and its inverse give the same numbers in reverse order, so one row stands for the pair {C, C^-1}. The number of rows is therefore (h+1)/2, where h is the number of properly primitive classes of determinant p. There is one genus, so h is odd.

1613 (≡ 5 mod 8): rows '1.13.13' and '4.23.31.19.52.17.61.4'. My check of the second row:
- (4,39,-23), (-23,30,31), (31,32,-19), (-19,25,52), (52,27,-17), (-17,24,61), (61,37,-4), and back to 4.
- So h = 3.

1489: rows starting 1 and 3, the latter beginning (3,38,-15). So h = 3.

1601: rows 1 / 8.29.40.31.47.8.. / 16.5.61.16.. / 32.41.25.37.40.19.43.32. The right column reads 0.7, 1.6, 2.5, 3.4. My check of the cycles:
- (8,37,-29), (-29,21,40), (40,19,-31), (-31,12,47), (47,35,-8);
- (16,39,-5), (-5,36,61), (61,25,-16);
- (32,17,-41), (-41,24,25), (25,26,-37), (-37,11,40), (40,29,-19), (-19,28,43), (43,15,-32).
No properly primitive form can have a = 2 or 4 here, because p ≡ 1 mod 8 forces c even. So 8, 16, 32 are the smallest 2-power leading coefficients. The pairs k.(7-k) say that h = 7 and the class group is cyclic of order 7, with the three rows being C^{±1}, C^{±2}, C^{±3} for C the class of (8,37,-29). This is consistent with the ideal-theoretic reading (my addition):
- (8,37,-29) extends to the prime above 2 in Q(sqrt p);
- (16,39,-5) extends to its square;
- (32,17,-41) extends to its cube.
The same notation appears on the neighbouring pages: 2029 has 0.7 ... 3.4, and 1901 and 1129 have 0.9 ... 4.5. The previous page summarises these counts ('46 with 1 class, 14 with 3, ...' for primes between 2000 and 3000).

PURPOSE. The page is a tabulation of class numbers, with the cyclic structure noted where h > 1, of properly primitive forms of positive prime determinant p ≡ 1 mod 4. It belongs to Gauss's empirical study behind Disq. Art. 303-304, including his remark on how often a single class per genus occurs for positive determinants. The previous page also links the period to the solution of P^2 - pQ^2 = ±1. The boxed '22.3' at the bottom is probably a date (22 March [1798]) or a page or count mark; this is uncertain.
errors: 1789, row 2: the transcription has '35.20.33.21'. The recurrence gives Q13 = (1789-27^2)/20 = 53, so the entry should be 53. It is either a misread 5/3 or a Gauss slip.
1789, row 3: the transcription has '51.13.67'. The recurrence gives (1789-32^2)/51 = 15, so the entry should be 15.
1789, row 4: the transcription has '12.59.5.5'. The recurrence gives (1789-31^2)/12 = 69, so the entry should be 69.
1609, row 2: '45.32.19.31' should be 45.32.39.31, since (1609-19^2)/32 = 39. This may be a genuine slip by Gauss (19 is the P-value at that step) or a misreading.
1493: the first entry is read as 44, but Q1 = 1493 - 38^2 = 49. The rest of the row (28, 43, 19, 28, 31, 4, 67, 7, 7) is correct. This is most likely a transcription misreading of 49.

Apart from these isolated entries, every row I recomputed is correct. These are 1801 (complete), 1777 (complete), 1669 (complete), 1609 (complete), 1493, 1613 row 2, 1601 (all rows) and the opening entries of all other primes. None of the possible slips affects the terminal repeated value, the derived two-square representation, or the class counts.

results.what: Cycles (periods) of reduced forms of determinant p, i.e. the denominators Q_n in the continued-fraction expansion of sqrt(p), computed for all primes p ≡ 1 mod 4 from 1489 to 1801.
results.modern_name: Continued-fraction / reduction-cycle algorithm for indefinite binary quadratic forms (infrastructure of real quadratic orders)
results.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1770s) for continued fractions of quadratic irrationals and reduction; Gauss, Disquisitiones (1801), Art. 183-187, for cycles of forms

results.what: The palindromic odd period has a central pair of equal Q's, giving p = b^2 + a^2 at the midpoint of the cycle.
results.modern_name: Legendre's continued-fraction method for writing p ≡ 1 mod 4 as a sum of two squares
results.usually_credited_to: Legendre (Essai sur la théorie des nombres, 1798); related ideas in Euler and Lagrange

results.what: Counting cycles to get the number of properly primitive classes for prime determinants: h = 1, or 3 for 1613 and 1489, or 7 for 1601. For 1601 the classes are labelled C^k / C^{7-k}, showing a cyclic class group of order 7 generated by the class of (8,37,-29).
results.modern_name: Class numbers and class-group structure of real quadratic orders Z[sqrt p] (tables of h(4p))
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Disquisitiones Art. 303-304; class-number tables in the Nachlass, Werke II)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a working sheet for Gauss's known tables of class numbers of positive determinants, computed in 1798 by the cycle method later published in the Disquisitiones. The by-product two-square representations are Legendre's (contemporary) method. The only slightly notable detail is the explicit cyclic labelling 0.7/1.6/2.5/3.4 of the non-principal classes for 1601, but Gauss's awareness of class-group composition structure is well known.

checkable.asserts: Gauss's row for 1801 equals the continued-fraction denominators Q_n of sqrt(1801), up to the central repeat (sqrt here is integer-floor via int(sqrt(p))).
For each prime, p minus the square of the terminal repeated number is a perfect square, i.e. the midpoint of the cycle gives p as a sum of two squares.
The cycles 16,5,61 and 32,41,25,37,40,19,43 of determinant 1601 are correct.
The second cycle for 1613 (4.23.31.19.52.17.61.4) is correct, so 1613 has 3 properly primitive classes.
The correct values at the positions where the transcription shows 33, 13, 59 (1789), 53, 19 (1609), 47 (1669) and 44 (1493).
The apparently struck-out 44 in the 1621 row is in fact a correct and necessary entry of the period.

transcription_corrections: 1801, row 2: the item marked '[?]' between 7 and 51 is an ink blot, not a number. The sequence is ...40.7.51.32.45...
1621: '[-44-]' is not a deletion of a wrong value. The 44 is a correct and needed entry (15.44.33); any stroke is incidental or a re-inking.
1493: the first entry should probably be read '49' (1493-38^2 = 49), not '44'.
1789: the entries transcribed as 33 (row 2), 13 (row 3) and 59 (row 4) should be 53, 15 and 69 by recomputation. They are likely misreadings of Gauss's 5/3/6 shapes; if not, they are Gauss's slips.
1609: the entries transcribed '53' (row 1) and '19' (row 2) should be 55 and 39 by recomputation. The brace near '25.}45' is a marginal mark, not a number.
1601: the right column '0.7, 1.6, 2.5, 3.4' gives class-exponent pairs (C^k, C^{7-k}) for the four rows. The '3.4' at the end of the last row belongs to this column, not to the sequence.
1753: the final symbol after '27.27' is '&c' (or a blot), not the number 8.
